repos.name: ayghri / i-have-adhd
repos.description: A skill to stop your coding agent from burying the answer. ADHD-friendly output.

summary.goal: i-have-adhd is a skill/plugin for AI coding assistants that reformats responses to be ADHD-friendly: action-first, with numbered steps, and without filler phrases like "Hope this helps!". No ADHD diagnosis is needed to use it.
summary.usage: Install by pasting the provided prompt, which references https://github.com/ayghri/i-have-adhd and the repo's AGENTS.md, into your CLI, or follow INSTALL.md. In Claude Code, manage it with commands such as `claude plugin install i-have-adhd@i-have-adhd`, then restart and reinvoke `/i-have-adhd`; it may also work with other AGENTS.md-compatible assistants, though the README does not fully specify this.
summary.pros: The README's before/after example shows a rambling, hedge-filled explanation replaced by a direct command, numbered edit steps, and one concrete next action. Its 10 stated rules also cap lists at 5 items, require specific time estimates, and suppress tangents, preambles, and closing remarks.
summary.cons: Customizing the skill appears to require forking the repository, editing SKILL.md, and running several plugin commands to remove the upstream copy before adding the fork, since fork and upstream share the same name—a multi-step process that could risk naming conflicts if not followed carefully.
summary.fit: This tool seems best suited to developers using Claude Code, or possibly other AGENTS.md-compatible coding assistants, who prefer terse, action-first responses over exploratory or hedged explanations. It is distributed under the MIT license.

repos.name: Tencent / teamai-cli
repos.description: Make Every Team AI Native

summary.goal: TeamAI (teamai-cli) is a CLI that manages a team's skills, rules, MCP configuration, and accumulated knowledge, distributing them across AI coding agents including Claude Code, Codex, CodeBuddy, WorkBuddy, OpenCode, and Cursor.
summary.usage: Install with `npm install -g teamai-cli`, then an admin creates a shared git repository and runs `teamai init https://github.com/yourorg/yourrepo`; team members run the same `teamai init` command (optionally with `--scope user`) to sync resources, and use `teamai pull`/`teamai push` to receive or contribute updates.
summary.pros: Resources sync automatically to local AI tools without manual syncing, and code-relationship extraction relies on a pure-JavaScript WASM tree-sitter parser, so no native toolchain is required; a fallback heuristic track covers additional languages if AST parsing is unavailable.
summary.cons: The Team Context and Team Improvement layers are labeled beta, and the Models capability is not implemented for every provider yet, so some functionality may still be evolving or provider-specific coverage may be incomplete.
summary.fit: The tool appears best suited to teams already working across several of the listed AI agents and git hosts (GitHub, GitLab, GitCode, CNB, TGit, or a private Git service), since setup requires an admin to create a shared repo and grant members write access.

repos.name: obra / superpowers
repos.description: An agentic skills framework & software development methodology that works.

summary.goal: Superpowers is described as a complete software development methodology for coding agents, built on composable skills paired with initial instructions that ensure the agent invokes them automatically.
summary.usage: Installation of Superpowers is harness-specific; for Claude Code, run `/plugin install superpowers@claude-plugins-official` from the official marketplace, or register a separate marketplace with `/plugin marketplace add obra/superpowers-marketplace` followed by `/plugin install superpowers@superpowers-marketplace`. Once installed, skills like brainstorming, writing-plans, and test-driven-development activate automatically to guide design, planning, and RED-GREEN-REFACTOR implementation.
summary.pros: The skills library covers testing, debugging, collaboration, and meta workflows, and the documented basic workflow emphasizes test-first development, code review between tasks, and evidence-based verification before completion. It supports multiple coding agents, including Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and Gemini CLI, among other supported harnesses.
summary.cons: Because installation differs by harness, using Superpowers with more than one coding agent requires installing it separately for each, which could add setup and update overhead.
summary.fit: This methodology appears best suited to teams already working with one of the supported coding agents who want a structured, mandatory design-to-implementation workflow, and may be less fitting for those seeking a lightweight, optional process.

repos.name: pascalorg / editor
repos.description: Create and share 3D architectural projects.

summary.goal: Pascal Editor is a 3D building editor built with React Three Fiber and WebGPU, organized as a monorepo containing reusable editor packages (@pascal-app/core, @pascal-app/viewer, @pascal-app/editor, @pascal-app/nodes), a standalone application, an @pascal-app/cli installer, and an @pascal-app/mcp server for AI-host integration.
summary.usage: A persistent local installation can be created without cloning the repository by running `npx @pascal-app/cli editor` with Node.js 22.13 or newer, which starts the editor and an authenticated MCP service. For monorepo development, `bun install` followed by `bun dev` builds the packages and starts the editor's development server.
summary.pros: The package separation lets @pascal-app/core (schemas and state), @pascal-app/viewer (rendering), @pascal-app/editor (tools and UI), @pascal-app/nodes (built-in definitions), @pascal-app/cli, and @pascal-app/mcp be used or extended independently. The @pascal-app/mcp package exposes scene tools, resources, and prompts to MCP-compatible AI hosts, and the editor supports plugin-based extension using the same manifest format as built-in node kinds.
summary.cons: The npm beta tag currently resolves to @pascal-app/cli@1.0.0-beta.1, which predates the read-only furniture candidate feature described in the repository; using that capability requires manually installing a GitHub prerelease archive and verifying its SHA-256 checksum rather than a standard npm install.
summary.fit: Given its React Three Fiber and WebGPU rendering, node-based scene model, and MCP-based AI agent tooling, the project appears best suited for developers building or extending 3D architectural or interior layout editors with AI-assisted workflows, rather than general-purpose 3D applications.

repos.name: earthtojake / text-to-cad
repos.description: A library of agent skills for CAD, CAE and CAM

summary.goal: text-to-cad is a library of agent skills for CAD, CAE, and CAM that generates, inspects, sources, slices, and hands off CAD and robot-description artifacts from local project files (lines 16, 37-39). Documented skills include CAD, DXF, URDF, SRDF, SDF, G-code, and Bambu Labs (lines 69-81).
summary.usage: Install the skills with `npx skills add earthtojake/text-to-cad`, described as the preferred installation path (lines 92-99); each skill's `requirements.txt` pins the `cadgen` release it was published with (line 86). Plugin installs are also available for Codex, Claude Code, and Grok Build, e.g. `claude plugin install cad@text-to-cad` (lines 112-130).
summary.pros: The library bundles CAD, DXF, URDF, SRDF, SDF, slicing, and print-job skills together, with the CAD skill exporting STEP plus STL, 3MF, and GLB (line 71). Re-running the add command refreshes existing skills and installs any newly released ones (lines 101-102).
summary.cons: `npx skills update` only refreshes skills already in the lockfile, so it can silently miss skills added in newer releases; `npx skills add` covers updates instead (lines 101-105). The Codex plugin path requires Codex 0.142.0 or newer, with older versions skipping it silently (lines 118, 123-125).
summary.fit: Given its plugin installs for Codex, Claude Code, and Grok Build, the project seems aimed at teams using AI coding agents for CAD and robot-description work (lines 112-115). The CAD skill's dependencies are pinned for Python 3.11+ (line 25) under the MIT license (line 23).

repos.name: cathrynlavery / diagram-design
repos.description: 38 editorial diagram types for Claude Code, Codex, and Pi. Self-contained HTML + SVG. No shadows. No Mermaid slop.

summary.goal: Diagram Design is a Claude Code skill, also usable with Codex, Factory Droid, and Pi, that generates editorial-style diagrams. It documents 39 diagram types—including architecture, flowchart, and sequence diagrams—produced as self-contained HTML and SVG files rather than generic Mermaid-style output.
summary.usage: Install it in Claude Code by running /plugin marketplace add cathrynlavery/diagram-design followed by /plugin install diagram-design@diagram-design, then request diagrams in natural language or via commands such as /diagram-design:export-diagram. Codex, Factory Droid, Pi, and OpenCode each have separate documented install steps.
summary.pros: Diagrams ship as static, self-contained HTML with no build step required to view them, and each SVG includes accessibility attributes such as role="img" and a resolving aria-labelledby. An optional onboarding flow extracts a website's color palette and fonts, checking WCAG AA contrast before applying them to new diagrams.
summary.cons: PNG export requires an additional one-time setup step beyond the default HTML output: pip install playwright && playwright install chromium. This dependency is unrelated to viewing or creating the standard self-contained HTML diagrams.
summary.fit: The skill fits documentation and technical-diagram workflows for AI coding agents that support Claude's Agent Skills format, matching diagrams to an existing brand's colors and fonts. It is presented as unsuited for quick unicode diagrams, plain lists, before/after comparisons, or single-box diagrams, suggesting narrower use outside structured technical documentation.

repos.name: TauricResearch / TradingAgents
repos.description: TradingAgents: Multi-Agents LLM Financial Trading Framework

summary.goal: TradingAgents is a multi-agent LLM financial trading framework (built with LangGraph) that mirrors a trading firm: fundamentals, sentiment, news, and technical analysts feed a trader and risk-management/portfolio-manager team that decides trade actions, for research into multi-agent market analysis.
summary.usage: Clone the TradingAgents repo (`git clone https://github.com/TauricResearch/TradingAgents.git`), create a Python 3.12 environment, and run `pip install .` (or use Docker). Export API keys for your chosen LLM provider, then launch the interactive CLI with `tradingagents` (or `python -m cli.main`), or import `TradingAgentsGraph` in Python and call `.propagate(ticker, date)` to get a decision.
summary.pros: TradingAgents supports many LLM providers (OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, xAI, DeepSeek, Qwen, GLM, MiniMax, OpenRouter, Ollama, Azure OpenAI) and works with any market covered by Yahoo Finance using exchange-suffixed tickers. It also offers an opt-in checkpoint-resume feature so an interrupted run can continue from its last completed step.
summary.cons: Because it is LLM-driven, the README states two runs on the same ticker/date can differ due to non-deterministic sampling and changing live news/social data; lowering temperature helps only with non-reasoning models, since curated reasoning models largely ignore it. TradingAgents is described as research-oriented and explicitly not financial, investment, or trading advice (https://tauric.ai/disclaimer/).
summary.fit: TradingAgents seems best suited to researchers and developers exploring multi-agent LLM trading analysis rather than users wanting a production strategy with guaranteed returns. Backtest results are stated as not guaranteed to match any published figure, so performance-critical or real-money use would likely need further validation.

repos.name: liquidslr / system-design-notes
repos.description: Notes of the book System Desgin Interview - An Insider's Guide

summary.goal: This repository provides personal notes based on the books "System Design Interview - An Insider's Guide" Volume 1 and Volume 2 (2nd Edition) by Alex Xu, covering common system design interview topics.
summary.usage: The repository is organized into 28 chapter folders (e.g., Rate Limiter, Consistent Hashing, Chat System) that can be browsed directly on GitHub, and a compiled version of the notes is available at https://pagefy.io/system-design/system-design-interview-by-alex-xu.
summary.pros: Beyond the chapter notes, the repository curates additional external resources by topic, including engineering blog posts from companies like Discord, Netflix, and Dropbox, which may offer readers broader context on real-world system implementations.
summary.cons: The README explicitly states these notes are a work in progress, so chapter content and coverage may currently be incomplete or subject to change.
summary.fit: Given its structure around the well-known System Design Interview book series, this project appears best suited for engineers or students preparing for system design interviews rather than as a standalone reference or software tool.

repos.name: openai / plugins
repos.description: OpenAI Plugins

summary.goal: This repository provides a curated collection of example plugins for Codex, demonstrating how developers can build plugin bundles for tools such as Figma, Notion, SwiftUI-based iOS/macOS apps, web apps, Expo, Netlify, Remotion, and Google Slides.
summary.usage: Each plugin is organized under plugins/<name>/ and must include a .codex-plugin/plugin.json manifest, with optional companion files like skills/, .app.json, .mcp.json, agents/, commands/, hooks.json, and assets/. The default marketplace configuration is located at .agents/plugins/marketplace.json, pointing to the plugins/ directory.
summary.pros: The repository offers several richer, real-world examples spanning design (Figma), knowledge work (Notion), mobile/desktop development (build-ios-apps, build-macos-apps, expo), and web deployment (build-web-apps, netlify), giving developers multiple reference implementations for learning plugin structure.
summary.cons: Users authenticating with an API key appear to rely on a separate marketplace file (.agents/plugins/api_marketplace.json) rather than the default one, which suggests the plugin discovery setup may differ depending on login method and could require additional configuration awareness.
summary.fit: This repository appears best suited for developers already working within the Codex ecosystem who want reference examples for building or extending plugins across design, productivity, and app-development domains, rather than for those seeking a single standalone tool.

repos.name: freestylefly / awesome-gpt-image-2
repos.description: Prompt as Code | GPT-Image2 工业级提示词引擎与模板库，530+ 个案例逆向工程，20+ 套工业级模板，并提炼出Skills，持续更新中

summary.goal: awesome-gpt-image-2 is a Prompt-as-Code repository and template library for the GPT-Image2 image-generation model, packaging 500+ reverse-engineered cases (a badge cites 544 cases) and 20+ industrial prompt templates across categories like UI, posters, and branding, released under the MIT License.
summary.usage: Browse the case gallery and templates directly in the repo (docs/gallery.md, docs/templates.md) or via the companion site at https://gpt-image2.canghe.ai. To use the bundled agent skill in Claude Code, Codex, or Cursor, install the CLI with `npm install -g gpt-image-2-style-library` and run `gpt-image-2-style-library install all`, which writes the skill to local agent folders such as ~/.claude/skills.
summary.pros: The library organizes prompts into an atomic schema (subjects, lighting, materials, layout) intended to be workflow-friendly for agents, scripts, and automation, and it groups 544 cases into 13 categories (e.g., UI, charts, photography) with a matching template page for each. The agent skill also plugs into multiple tool ecosystems (npm, GitHub Packages, Claude Code plugin marketplace).
summary.cons: Enabling the companion website's generation and auth features requires a nontrivial setup: multiple sequential Supabase SQL migrations plus Vercel environment variables for Supabase, Stripe, and Google Analytics. The README also notes the GPT Image 2.5 spotlight section only demonstrates recreated examples and 'does not add live 2.5 image generation,' and that original generation conditions for those examples remain unverified.
summary.fit: Given its structured, agent-oriented prompt format, the project appears best suited to teams or individual developers building repeatable, script- or agent-driven GPT-Image2 image-generation workflows rather than users seeking a ready-to-run hosted generation service without additional backend setup.

repos.name: rohitg00 / ai-engineering-from-scratch
repos.description: Learn it. Build it. Ship it for others.

summary.goal: AI Engineering from Scratch is a free, open-source curriculum offering 523 lessons across 20 phases (~342 hours), teaching AI engineering in Python, TypeScript, Rust, and Julia. Each lesson produces a reusable artifact—a prompt, skill, agent, or MCP server—covering topics from math foundations through agent engineering and production infrastructure.
summary.usage: Clone the repository and run `git clone https://github.com/rohitg00/ai-engineering-from-scratch.git`, then `cd ai-engineering-from-scratch` and `python3 phases/00-setup-and-tooling/01-dev-environment/code/verify.py --route beginner` to verify setup. Alternatively, install an AI tutor into a compatible coding agent with `npx skills add rohitg00/ai-engineering-from-scratch`, which streams lessons without requiring a full clone for reading.
summary.pros: Each lesson follows a documented 'Build It / Use It' pattern: learners implement an algorithm from raw math before using the equivalent production library, reinforcing conceptual understanding. The curriculum is MIT-licensed and free, and core lessons also compile into a six-volume EPUB/PDF book series built from the same sources and attached to GitHub releases.
summary.cons: The included Claude Certification Academy is described as independent study material based on public exam objectives; it states it is not affiliated with Anthropic, does not reproduce live exam questions, and cannot guarantee a passing score, so results may vary for certification preparation.
summary.fit: A background-to-starting-point table suggests entry points ranging from Phase 0 (new programmers, ~306 hours) to Phase 14 (experienced engineers wanting agent engineering, ~60 hours), which appears to indicate the material is intended to suit learners at varied experience levels rather than beginners only.

repos.name: vastsa / PI-Desktop
repos.description: Local-first AI coding agent desktop: Electron + Rust host core + pi Agent Harness + user-installable plugins

summary.goal: PI-Desktop is a local-first desktop workspace for AI coding agents that lets users bring their own model and open any local project, without a PI-Desktop account or mandatory relay server. It is currently described as an Early Preview, meaning PI-Desktop's APIs, extension interfaces, and some desktop behaviors may continue to evolve.
summary.usage: To get started, a model is connected under Settings → Model configuration, a local project is opened, and Agent, Plan, or Goal mode is chosen before reviewing the result in PI-Desktop. Running PI-Desktop from source uses `git clone https://github.com/vastsa/PI-Desktop.git`, `pnpm install`, `cargo build -p host-core`, and `pnpm dev`; prebuilt packages are available from https://github.com/vastsa/PI-Desktop/releases/latest.
summary.pros: PI-Desktop lets users switch between multiple model providers per session, including OpenAI, Anthropic, local models, and OpenAI-compatible APIs, while routing privileged agent actions through a permission layer for review. It also supports extension through Skills, MCP servers, Subagents, and Plugins, letting users add tools, commands, and workspace panels.
summary.cons: PI-Desktop is documented as an Early Preview, so its APIs, extension interfaces, and desktop behaviors may continue to change. Linux builds of PI-Desktop require glibc 2.35 or newer (for example Ubuntu 22.04, Debian 12, or Fedora 36), so older distributions cannot load the bundled host.
summary.fit: PI-Desktop appears suited to developers wanting a model-agnostic, local-first coding workspace across macOS, Windows, and Linux. Building PI-Desktop from source requires Node.js >=22.19, pnpm >=10, and a stable Rust toolchain, which may add more setup effort than using a prebuilt release package.

repos.name: affaan-m / ECC
repos.description: The agent harness performance optimization system. Skills, instincts, memory, security, and research-first development for Claude Code, Codex, Opencode, Cursor and beyond.

summary.goal: ECC is an MIT-licensed open-source "agent harness operating system" that layers a coordinated engineering workflow (plan, test, implement, review, verify, remember, improve) onto coding agents. It is designed to work best with Claude Code today, includes a supported Codex sync path, and provides capability-limited adapters for other harnesses such as Cursor, OpenCode, Gemini, Zed, GitHub Copilot, Antigravity, and Qwen.
summary.usage: Install by running `npx ecc-universal setup` from a terminal, or from inside Claude Code run `/plugin marketplace add https://github.com/affaan-m/ECC` followed by `/plugin install ecc@ecc`. The universal setup requires Node.js 18 or newer, and the Claude plugin path additionally requires Git and Claude Code 2.1 or newer.
summary.pros: ECC bundles 68 specialized agents, 286 reusable skills, and 94 maintained command shims, plus a hooks/memory runtime, selectively installable rule packs, and a built-in AgentShield security scanner covering prompts, hooks, MCP configuration, permissions, and secrets.
summary.cons: The README directs users to check a support-status matrix before assuming feature parity across harnesses, and several non-Claude adapters (Cursor, OpenCode, GitHub Copilot, and others) are documented as beta, instruction-only, or experimental/minimal. It also notes the project currently ships weekly from a single maintainer across seven harnesses, which may suggest maintenance capacity is fairly concentrated.
summary.fit: ECC appears best suited to teams already using Claude Code who want a structured engineering workflow layered onto agent coding sessions, since that is described as the primary, most stable target. Teams relying mainly on other harnesses will likely get more limited, adapter-based functionality rather than full feature parity.

repos.name: DietrichGebert / ponytail
repos.description: Makes your AI agent think like the laziest senior dev in the room. The best code is the code you never wrote.

summary.goal: Ponytail is a rule-set/plugin for AI coding agents such as Claude Code and Codex that guides them toward minimal, non-over-engineered code. Before writing new code, it follows a priority ladder — skip unneeded code (YAGNI), reuse existing code, use the standard library, native platform features, or an installed dependency, or write one line — while never cutting validation, error handling, security, or accessibility.
summary.usage: Installation is host-specific; for Claude Code it requires two separate prompts: `/plugin marketplace add DietrichGebert/ponytail` followed by `/plugin install ponytail@ponytail`. Other hosts, such as Codex and GitHub Copilot CLI, have their own install commands. Slash commands like `/ponytail` and `/ponytail-review` switch between lite, full, ultra, and off intensity levels; a `PONYTAIL_DEFAULT_MODE` environment variable can set the default (full by default).
summary.pros: Benchmarks against a no-skill baseline, run on a real FastAPI + React repo using Claude Code with Haiku 4.5, report ponytail cutting lines of code by 54%, cost by 20%, and time by 27%, while keeping 100% safety — better than a bare 'YAGNI + one-liners' prompt, which dropped to 95% safety.
summary.cons: The Claude Code and Codex plugins rely on two Node.js lifecycle hooks, so `node` must be on PATH or always-on activation stays silent instead of erroring. The headline benchmark numbers come from a small sample (n=4) on one model (Haiku 4.5) and one repo, so the measured gains may not generalize to other codebases or models.
summary.fit: The project reportedly works with 20 agent hosts per its badge, including Claude Code, Codex, GitHub Copilot CLI, Gemini CLI, and OpenCode. The `/ponytail` slash commands need a 'skill-capable host'; instruction-only adapters like Cursor, Windsurf, Cline, Copilot Chat, Kiro, and Antigravity load the always-on ruleset but without the commands.

repos.name: fmtlib / fmt
repos.description: A modern formatting library

summary.goal: {fmt} is an open-source C++ formatting library described in its README as a fast and safe alternative to C stdio and C++ iostreams, implementing the C++20 std::format and C++23 std::print interfaces.
summary.usage: It is used by including a header such as `#include <fmt/core.h>` and calling functions like `fmt::print("Hello, world!\n");` to format and print text; documentation is hosted at https://fmt.dev.
summary.pros: The README reports fmt can be tens of percent to 20–30 times faster than sprintf and iostreams for numeric formatting, with a single-threaded file-writing example cited as up to 9 times faster than fprintf; it also uses the Dragonbox algorithm for IEEE 754 floating-point formatting with correct rounding, offers compile-time format-string checking, and ships under a permissive MIT license with no external dependencies.
summary.cons: Benchmark figures in the README, measured on one specific machine (an Apple M5 Max running macOS 26.6.2 with Apple Clang 21.0.0), show optimized-build compile times of about 5.1 seconds for fmt 12.2 headers versus 1.6 seconds for plain printf and 49.1 seconds for Boost Format 1.92, so fmt adds measurable compile-time overhead compared to printf, though results may differ on other compilers or platforms.
summary.fit: Based on the notable adopters it lists, including ClickHouse, MongoDB, PyTorch, and Windows Terminal, fmt appears best suited to C++ projects that need high-performance, type-safe text formatting, though its fit for minimal-footprint or embedded contexts is not directly addressed.

repos.name: tt-a1i / archify
repos.description: Agent skill for beautiful, verifiable architecture, workflow, sequence, data-flow, and lifecycle diagrams—self-contained HTML with motion and crisp export.

summary.goal: Archify is a Node.js rendering and validation system that turns a codebase or system description into an interactive system map, producing typed JSON IR that Archify deterministically compiles into HTML/SVG for Cursor, Claude Code, Codex CLI, and OpenCode.
summary.usage: Install globally with `npx skills add tt-a1i/archify -g`, then describe a system directly in agent chat—no repository is required—or ask the agent to analyze a repository and generate a diagram. Repository commands such as `node archify/bin/archify.mjs compare architecture base.json head.json architecture-delta.html --json` support before/after architecture comparison.
summary.pros: Archify provides 5 diagram types with 4 presets and dark/light themes, an Architecture Delta mode that compares validated Before/Delta/After snapshots with a machine receipt, and atomic schema, layout, HTML/SVG, and route validation before delivering a self-contained HTML file with PNG, SVG, WebM, and share-card exports.
summary.cons: Automatic Mermaid parsing, general-purpose auto-layout, hosted sharing, and WYSIWYG editing are documented as intentionally outside the current scope, and the optional deployment-ownership profile fails closed—without inspecting live infrastructure—whenever authored owners, region placement, private database scope, or named crossings are missing.
summary.fit: Archify appears best suited to teams already using Cursor, Claude Code, Codex CLI, or OpenCode who want in-chat architecture communication artifacts or PR-time architecture review, rather than users seeking a general-purpose drawing editor, Mermaid theme, or hosted diagram sharing service.

repos.name: mattpocock / skills
repos.description: Skills for Real Engineers. Straight from my .agents directory.

summary.goal: mattpocock/skills is a collection of agent skills intended for real software engineering work rather than casual "vibe coding." The skills target common failure modes when working with coding agents: misalignment on requirements, overly verbose agent output, non-working code, and growing codebase complexity.
summary.usage: The skills can be installed as a managed Claude Code plugin with `claude plugins install mattpocock-skills` (or `/plugin install mattpocock-skills` inside a session), which updates automatically, or copied as editable files into a project using `npx skills@latest add mattpocock/skills`. After installing, run `/setup-matt-pocock-skills` once per repository to configure the issue tracker, triage labels, and documentation location.
summary.pros: Skills are described as small, adaptable, and composable, and work with any model. They are split into user-invoked skills (e.g. grill-me, tdd, code-review) and model-invoked skills that the agent can reach for automatically. The set covers practices such as test-driven development, code review, domain modeling, and architecture review.
summary.cons: Users must choose one installation path: installing both the Claude Code plugin and the skills.sh copy results in every skill being duplicated. The skills.sh version places editable files directly in the project, so keeping them current requires manually running `npx skills update`, rather than receiving automatic updates.
summary.fit: This project appears best suited to engineers who already use Claude Code, Codex, or similar coding agents and want structured, adaptable workflows for real applications, in contrast to fully automated planning frameworks like GSD, BMAD, or Spec-Kit, which are described as taking away control from the developer.

repos.name: blader / humanizer
repos.description: Agent skill that removes signs of AI-generated writing from text

summary.goal: Humanizer is a Markdown-based skill that rewrites AI-sounding text so it reads as if written by a person, without changing what the text says. According to the README, it works with any agent that supports skills.
summary.usage: Install it with the Skills CLI using `npx skills add blader/humanizer --global` for a global install, or omit `--global` for a project-only install; the skill responds to `/humanizer`. On Claude Code 2.1.142 or newer, it can instead be installed as a plugin with `/plugin marketplace add blader/humanizer` and `/plugin install humanizer@humanizer`, responding to `/humanizer:humanizer`. Claude Desktop requires a manual install by downloading the repo as a ZIP or copying SKILL.md into the agent's skill folder.
summary.pros: The rewrite process shows its work: an initial draft, a short critique, and a final version. It edits only prose, leaving code, data, frontmatter, and link targets unchanged, and the README states it does not invent facts, asking for missing details instead. It also supports voice matching from a writing sample, and organizes its checks into 25 numbered patterns ordered by strength and frequency.
summary.cons: Several patterns are documented as 'weak alone,' meaning they justify an edit only when multiple tells appear together in a passage, since a careful writer may use any one deliberately; this suggests some rewrite decisions may need human judgment in ambiguous cases.
summary.fit: This tool appears suited to users of skill-supporting agents such as Claude Code or Claude Desktop who want a documented, pattern-based way to reduce AI-sounding phrasing while preserving factual content; the README does not indicate support for agents lacking skills capability.

repos.name: ChromeDevTools / chrome-devtools-mcp
repos.description: Chrome DevTools for coding agents

summary.goal: chrome-devtools-mcp (Chrome DevTools for agents) is a Model-Context-Protocol (MCP) server that lets coding agents such as Antigravity, Claude, Cursor, or Copilot control and inspect a live Chrome browser, with a CLI also provided for use without MCP.
summary.usage: An MCP client is configured to run `npx -y chrome-devtools-mcp@latest` to start the chrome-devtools-mcp server; for basic browser tasks only, the `--slim` and `--headless` flags can be added. A first test prompt asking to check the performance of a URL confirms the browser opens and records a trace.
summary.pros: chrome-devtools-mcp uses Chrome DevTools to record traces and extract performance insights, supports advanced browser debugging such as analyzing network requests, screenshots, and source-mapped console messages, and relies on Puppeteer for reliable automation that automatically waits for action results.
summary.cons: Using chrome-devtools-mcp requires Node.js LTS, a current stable version of Chrome, and npm installed beforehand, and it officially supports only Google Chrome and Chrome for Testing, so other Chromium-based browsers may show unexpected behavior.
summary.fit: chrome-devtools-mcp appears suited for developers building agentic tooling who want an integrated browser subagent for automation, debugging, and performance analysis, though by default it collects usage statistics and can send trace URLs to Google's CrUX API unless disabled with flags.

repos.name: heygen-com / hyperframes
repos.description: Write HTML. Render video. Built for agents.

summary.goal: HyperFrames is an open-source framework for turning HTML, CSS, media, and seekable animations into deterministic MP4 videos. It can be used locally via a CLI, from AI coding agents through skills, or as the rendering core behind hosted authoring workflows.
summary.usage: Skills are installed with `npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes`; a project can also be scaffolded and rendered manually with `npx hyperframes init my-video`, `npx hyperframes preview`, and `npx hyperframes render`. Node.js 22+ and FFmpeg are listed as requirements.
summary.pros: Compositions are plain HTML with data attributes, so no React is required. Rendering is deterministic — the same input produces the same output — which suits CI and automated pipelines. The project is Apache 2.0 licensed with no per-render fees or commercial-use thresholds mentioned.
summary.cons: Running HyperFrames requires Node.js 22+ and FFmpeg to be installed beforehand. Cloning the full repository for development additionally requires Git LFS, since golden regression-test video baselines total roughly 240 MB, adding extra setup steps not needed for basic CLI usage.
summary.fit: HyperFrames appears best suited to developers and AI coding agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Codex, among others) that need HTML-based, deterministic video generation for things like product launches or PR walkthroughs. It is described as used in production at HeyGen, which may suggest reasonable production readiness, though broader adoption details are limited.

repos.name: mksglu / context-mode
repos.description: Context window optimization for AI coding agents. Sandboxes tool output (98% reduction), persists session memory, and   enforces routing across 17 platforms via MCP + hooks.

summary.goal: Context Mode is an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server built for AI coding agents. Its documented goal is reducing how much raw tool output — such as file reads, web fetches, and command results — enters the model's context window, while also preserving session state such as edited files and pending tasks across conversation compaction.
summary.usage: Claude Code users install it as a plugin with `/plugin marketplace add mksglu/context-mode` followed by `/plugin install context-mode@context-mode`, then restart Claude Code and run the diagnostics command to confirm the install. The documented prerequisite for this plugin path is Claude Code v1.0.33+; other supported clients register the same server as an MCP tool provider instead.
summary.pros: The README states that raw command output is processed inside an isolated sandbox subprocess, so only relevant results reach the conversation, with one documented example of a 315 KB session output reduced to about 5.4 KB — roughly a 98% reduction. It also documents no telemetry and no required account, since session data stays local.
summary.cons: On platforms without hook support, such as the Antigravity IDE and Zed, the README states that routing enforcement depends on a manually copied instruction file rather than automatic interception, and estimates this reaches only about 60% of the context savings achieved with hooks. The Cursor plugin is also documented as still awaiting marketplace review.
summary.fit: Based on the company logos presented as users, Context Mode appears suited to both individual developers and engineering teams working across MCP-compatible AI coding clients — the README documents support for 17 such clients plus an OpenClaw gateway integration. It is released under the Elastic License 2.0, a source-available license disallowing hosted or managed-service offerings.

repos.name: openai / skills
repos.description: Skills Catalog for Codex

summary.goal: This repository catalogs Agent Skills — folders of instructions, scripts, and resources — for use and distribution with the Codex AI agent platform. Skills package capabilities so teams and individuals can complete tasks in a repeatable way.
summary.usage: Skills in the `.system` folder install automatically in the latest Codex. Curated or experimental skills are installed via the `$skill-installer` command inside Codex, e.g. `$skill-installer gh-address-comments`, or by specifying a GitHub directory URL: `$skill-installer install https://github.com/openai/skills/tree/main/skills/.experimental/create-plan`. Codex must be restarted afterward for the skill to take effect.
summary.pros: Skills are reusable across projects ('write once, use everywhere') and installable with simple named commands through `$skill-installer`. System skills need no manual setup, and the Agent Skills format follows an open standard rather than a proprietary one.
summary.cons: The repository is explicitly marked deprecated, with current Codex skill and plugin examples redirected to the openai/plugins repository, so future updates or support for skills here appear uncertain. A Codex restart is also required after each install.
summary.fit: This repository likely suits existing Codex users wanting prepackaged, repeatable skills, though given the deprecation notice, those seeking current examples would probably be better served by openai/plugins instead. Licensing is defined per skill in its own LICENSE.txt file.

repos.name: coreyhaines31 / marketingskills
repos.description: Marketing skills for Claude Code and AI agents. CRO, copywriting, SEO, analytics, and growth engineering.

summary.goal: This repository offers a collection of AI agent skills for marketing tasks—conversion optimization, copywriting, SEO, analytics, and growth engineering. It targets technical marketers and founders using AI coding agents such as Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, Cursor, or Windsurf, and works with agents that support its skill format. Built by Corey Haines, it is MIT-licensed.
summary.usage: Skills install via `npx skills add coreyhaines31/marketingskills`, or through Claude Code's plugin system using `/plugin marketplace add coreyhaines31/marketingskills` followed by `/plugin install marketing-skills`. Once installed, users ask their agent for marketing help or invoke a skill directly, such as `/cro`.
summary.pros: The collection organizes 50 skills across categories like conversion optimization, copy, SEO, paid distribution, and retention. A `product-marketing` skill serves as a shared foundation other skills reportedly check first, suggesting the skills form an interconnected system rather than standalone scripts. It is free and MIT-licensed.
summary.cons: Upgrading from v1.x to v2.0 requires manually deleting stale old-named skill folders, since 17 skills were renamed and `page-cro` (plus `form-cro`) merged into `cro`, and the installer adds new skills alongside old ones instead of replacing them. Moving an existing product marketing context file to its new location and filename is also a manual step, though old paths reportedly still work as a fallback.
summary.fit: The skills suit technical marketers and founders using AI coding agents for marketing execution; a companion guide targets those newer to terminals and coding agents. Because installation steps focus mainly on Claude Code and a shared universal directory, support depth for other listed agents may vary in the documentation.

repos.name: THU-MAIC / OpenMAIC
repos.description: Open Multi-Agent Interactive Classroom — Get an immersive, multi-agent learning experience in just one click

summary.goal: OpenMAIC (Open Multi-Agent Interactive Classroom) is documented as an open-source AI platform that turns a topic or document into an interactive classroom, using multi-agent orchestration to generate slides, quizzes, interactive simulations, and project-based learning activities delivered by AI teachers and classmates. Released August 27, 2026, v1.0.0 adds a Pro workbench for agent-driven course building alongside the existing one-click generator.
summary.usage: Documented setup: clone with `git clone https://github.com/THU-MAIC/OpenMAIC.git`, run `pnpm install`, add at least one LLM provider API key to `.env.local`, then start the dev server with `pnpm dev` and open `http://localhost:3000`. Prerequisites listed are `Node.js >= 22.19` and `pnpm >= 10`; Docker Compose and Vercel deployment paths are also documented.
summary.pros: The README lists 20 built-in course-building skills, provider-neutral configuration for LLM, media, search, and storage backends, export to editable .pptx or interactive HTML, and an interface covering 12 locales across 11 languages.
summary.cons: The documented server-backed persistence setup notes that its NEXT_PUBLIC_PERSISTENCE_TOKEN compiles into the public JavaScript bundle with no confidentiality or user isolation, so that configuration is described as suitable only for localhost or trusted-network, single-user deployments.
summary.fit: Based on the setup instructions, OpenMAIC seems best suited to users able to supply at least one LLM provider API key and comfortable running a Node.js/pnpm project locally, via Docker, or on Vercel; production multi-user deployments would seemingly need the additional authentication work the persistence documentation flags.

repos.name: Imbad0202 / academic-research-skills
repos.description: Academic Research Skills for Claude Code: research → write → review → revise → finalize

summary.goal: Academic Research Skills (ARS) is a suite of Claude Code skills covering the academic research pipeline from initial research to publication, currently at version v3.21.2. It is positioned as a human-in-the-loop tool that automates supporting tasks—reference gathering, citation formatting, and consistency checks—while leaving question framing, methodology choice, and interpretation to the researcher.
summary.usage: Install through the Claude Code CLI, VS Code, or JetBrains (Claude Code v3.7.0+) using `/plugin marketplace add Imbad0202/academic-research-skills` followed by `/plugin install academic-research-skills`. Set the `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` environment variable. After installing, running `/ars-plan` starts a guided Socratic dialogue for structuring a paper; Pandoc and tectonic are optional for DOCX/PDF output.
summary.pros: The suite bundles four skills: a 13-agent Deep Research skill with Socratic and PRISMA review modes, a 12-agent Academic Paper writer offering style calibration and LaTeX/APA output, a 7-agent multi-perspective Paper Reviewer, and a 10-stage Pipeline orchestrator with mandatory integrity checkpoints and citation verification against bibliographic indexes such as Semantic Scholar and Crossref.
summary.cons: The Paper Reviewer's live output is documented as remaining 'NOT_CALIBRATED,' so no numerical score currently appears to map to accept or reject decisions. The optional reproducibility lockfile is described as configuration documentation rather than a replay guarantee, since LLM outputs are not byte-reproducible, and integrity checks do not appear able to confirm that reported procedures were actually performed.
summary.fit: Because the project is released under CC BY-NC 4.0, it appears intended for individual academic researchers and non-commercial use rather than commercial products. Its plugin-based installation suggests it is best suited to users already working inside the Claude Code CLI, VS Code, or JetBrains environment.

repos.name: every-app / open-seo
repos.description: Open source alternative to Semrush and Ahrefs

summary.goal: OpenSEO is described as an open source, pay-as-you-go alternative to Semrush and Ahrefs. It is designed for use with AI agents such as Claude Code, OpenClaw, and Hermes, exposing an MCP server and pre-built Agent Skills so agents can perform SEO tasks using OpenSEO's data.
summary.usage: A hosted version can be tried free at openseo.so, with an optional $10/month subscription. For self-hosting, OpenSEO documents a simple Docker setup for personal testing and a Cloudflare setup, recommended for internet-facing, multi-device or team use, which works on Cloudflare's free plan. Both require a separately obtained DataForSEO API key. Contributors can add a documented skill with `npx skills add every-app/open-seo --skill simple-issue-description`.
summary.pros: No recurring subscription is required for self-hosted use, since users bring their own DataForSEO API key and pay DataForSEO only for what they consume. A modern, simple UI focuses on specific workflows, and users can fork the project to build custom tools.
summary.cons: Self-hosted access to SEO data depends on a separately paid DataForSEO API key, so functionality is not available out of the box. Docker self-hosting appears intended mainly for personal testing, with Cloudflare recommended instead unless a user is already confident self-hosting other apps. Plans to simplify hosting on platforms like Railway, Coolify, or Dokploy in coming months suggest current support for those platforms may be more limited.
summary.fit: OpenSEO appears suited to individuals or small teams wanting SEO workflows such as keyword research, rank tracking, competitor insights, backlinks, site audits, and AI visibility, combined with AI-agent integration. The free trial and Docker path seem suited to personal evaluation, while Cloudflare, usable on a free plan, appears intended for team, internet-facing use.

repos.name: ruvnet / ruflo
repos.description: 🌊 The original agent meta-harness. Deploy intelligent multi-player swarms, coordinate autonomous workflows, and build conversational AI systems. Features adaptive memory, self-learning intelligence, RAG integration, and native Claude Code / Codex / Hermes and many more Integrated

summary.goal: Ruflo is presented as an agent meta-harness for Claude Code and Codex — an execution layer that adds specialized agents, swarm coordination, self-learning memory, and cross-machine agent federation on top of those tools.
summary.usage: The core install is `npx ruflo init`, which sets up the full CLI feature set (agents, MCP server, hooks); a lighter option adds Ruflo as a Claude Code plugin via the plugin marketplace. Ruflo can also register as an MCP server with `claude mcp add claude-flow -- npx ruflo@latest mcp start`.
summary.pros: The README lists 100+ specialized agents, multiple swarm coordination topologies, self-learning memory backed by an HNSW-indexed AgentDB, a marketplace of 33 native and 21 npm plugins, multi-provider LLM routing (Claude, GPT, Gemini, Cohere, Ollama), and security features such as AIDefence and CVE remediation.
summary.cons: The README documents two distinct install paths — a lightweight plugin install versus the full CLI install — with different files, MCP registration, and hooks; it also notes that MCP tool names differ between them (prefixed plugin tool names versus bare CLI tool names), which may require care when applying examples written for one path to the other.
summary.fit: Given its stated dependency on Claude Code and Codex and its emphasis on multi-agent orchestration, memory, and federation, Ruflo appears best suited to teams already using those tools who want production-grade coordination features, with the CLI install recommended for full, documented functionality.

repos.name: llvm / llvm-project
repos.description: The LLVM Project is a collection of modular and reusable compiler and toolchain technologies.

summary.goal: LLVM is a toolkit for building highly optimized compilers, optimizers, and run-time environments. Its core component, LLVM, provides the tools, libraries, and headers needed to process intermediate representations into object files, including an assembler, disassembler, bitcode analyzer, and bitcode optimizer. The project also includes the Clang frontend for compiling C, C++, Objective-C, and Objective-C++, along with the libc++ standard library and the LLD linker.
summary.usage: Building and running LLVM is documented on the Getting Started with LLVM page (https://llvm.org/docs/GettingStarted.html#getting-the-source-code-and-building-llvm), which covers obtaining the source and compiling the project. Contributors can follow the Contributing to LLVM guide (https://llvm.org/docs/Contributing.html) for guidance on submitting changes.
summary.pros: The project spans a full compiler toolchain, pairing the core LLVM libraries with the Clang frontend, libc++ standard library, and LLD linker. It displays OpenSSF Scorecard and Best Practices badges, and offers multiple community channels including Discourse forums, Discord chat, office hours, and regular sync-ups.
summary.cons: The README does not include inline build commands or version numbers; it instead directs readers to an external Getting Started page for source retrieval and compilation steps, which may require an extra navigation step before building can begin.
summary.fit: Given its focus on intermediate-representation processing, frontend compilation, and linking, LLVM appears suited for developers building custom compilers, language frontends, or optimized run-time tooling, though the README does not specify particular deployment scenarios or performance benchmarks.

repos.name: petergyang / no-ai-slop
repos.description: Removes 20+ patterns of AI slop from any piece of writing.

summary.goal: No AI Slop is a skill for removing 20+ documented patterns of AI-sounding writing—such as 'It's not X. It's Y.' or 'What nobody tells you'—while aiming to preserve the writer's own vocabulary, cadence, and humor.
summary.usage: Install it by pasting an instruction that references https://github.com/petergyang/no-ai-slop into ChatGPT, Claude Code, Codex, or a similar coding agent, or by running `npx skills add petergyang/no-ai-slop --skill no-ai-slop --global --yes`. After installing, run `/no-ai-slop (your writing)` to edit text, or add 'is this slop?' to only flag patterns without editing.
summary.pros: After editing, the skill lists the changes it made, and in detection mode it quotes each matched slop pattern directly instead of asserting whether AI wrote the text. It also checks fundamentals like active voice and concrete phrasing.
summary.cons: The detection mode appears to deliberately avoid judging whether AI actually wrote the text, focusing only on flagging slop patterns, which suggests it may not function as a general AI-content detector.
summary.fit: Based on its install paths, the skill seems intended for writers who already use ChatGPT, Claude Code, Codex, or a comparable coding agent, since setup depends on one of those tools or on npx.

repos.name: omacom / omarchy
repos.description: Beautiful, Modern & Opinionated Linux

summary.goal: Omarchy is presented as a Linux distribution created by DHH, described as "beautiful, fun & agentic," with more information available at https://omarchy.org.
summary.usage: Its documentation is organized in a manual/ directory, also mirrored at https://learn.omacom.io/2/the-omarchy-manual, covering topics such as Getting Started, Hotkeys, and the Omarchy CLI; since no separate installation command is given, setup and navigation appear to begin with the "Getting Started" and "Coming From Mac or Windows" manual pages.
summary.pros: It is released under the MIT License (https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT), and its manual spans roughly fifty pages covering applications, configuration, theming, hardware, security, and troubleshooting topics.
summary.cons: Because documentation is split across dozens of separate manual files rather than one consolidated guide, users may need to check multiple pages to piece together full setup or configuration details, and cross-platform users may need to rely on the separate "Windows VM" and "Mac support" pages, suggesting native support is Linux-centric.
summary.fit: Omarchy appears best suited to Linux users wanting a preconfigured desktop environment with built-in AI, development, and theming tools, though platform or hardware prerequisites beyond the listed manual topics are not specified.

repos.name: cursor / plugins
repos.description: Cursor plugin specification and official plugins

summary.goal: This repository (cursor/plugins) is an official marketplace of Cursor plugins for popular developer tools, frameworks, and SaaS products. Each plugin is a standalone directory at the repository root with its own `.cursor-plugin/plugin.json` manifest, and the plugins span categories such as Developer Tools, Productivity, and Integrations.
summary.usage: The repo is structured as a multi-plugin marketplace: a root `.cursor-plugin/marketplace.json` file lists all plugins, and each plugin directory contains its own `.cursor-plugin/plugin.json` manifest plus optional `skills/` (SKILL.md files), `rules/` (.mdc files), an `mcp.json` MCP server definition, and its own README, CHANGELOG, and LICENSE files.
summary.pros: The catalog is broad, covering code-review and orchestration tooling (e.g., PR review canvases, parallel-agent workflows) alongside SaaS integrations for email, calendar, CRM, meeting transcripts, and more. Author attribution is tracked per plugin via `plugin.json`, and the whole repository is released under the permissive MIT license.
summary.cons: Because every plugin ships as a `.cursor-plugin` manifest, the plugins likely depend on the Cursor editor/agent environment to function, though the README does not document a minimum Cursor version, installation command, or other setup requirements.
summary.fit: This project appears best suited for teams already working in Cursor who want to extend it with third-party SaaS connectors and developer-workflow plugins, rather than for users seeking a standalone application independent of the Cursor ecosystem.

repos.name: anthropics / claude-plugins-community
repos.description: Community plugin marketplace for Claude Cowork and Claude Code. Read-only mirror — submit plugins at clau.de/plugin-directory-submission.

summary.goal: Claude Plugins — Community is documented as a read-only mirror of the community plugin marketplace for Claude Cowork and Claude Code. The .claude-plugin/marketplace.json file lists plugins available for installation, synced nightly from Anthropic's internal review pipeline.
summary.usage: Plugins can be installed from claude.com/plugins/ for Claude Cowork, or through the Claude Code CLI, which requires first adding the marketplace and then installing a specific plugin by running `claude plugin marketplace add anthropics/claude-plugins-community` followed by `claude plugin install <plugin-name>@claude-community`.
summary.pros: Every listed plugin has passed automated security scanning and been approved for distribution before appearing in the marketplace. Submissions go through a single, centralized intake point at clau.de/plugin-directory-submission rather than ad hoc channels.
summary.cons: Because the marketplace list syncs only nightly from an internal pipeline, the visible plugin set may lag behind the actual review state by up to a day; exact update timing and discrepancy handling are not detailed in the source material.
summary.fit: This repository appears suited for users who want to browse and install pre-vetted plugins through the documented web interface or CLI, rather than contribute code directly, since pull requests opened against the repo are closed automatically.

repos.name: AprilNEA / OpenLogi
repos.description: ⚡️A native, local-first alternative to Logitech Options+, written in Rust 🦀 — remap buttons, DPI, and SmartShift over HID++. No account, no telemetry.

summary.goal: OpenLogi is a native, local-first alternative to Logitech Options+, written in Rust, that unlocks additional capabilities of Logitech mice, keyboards, and webcams over the HID++ and UVC protocols. It runs on macOS, Linux, and Windows and is currently under active development, so features and configuration may still change.
summary.usage: Before installing, quit Logi Options+, since the two applications cannot share HID++ access to the same receiver. On macOS 13 or later, install via Homebrew with `brew install --cask openlogi`. Linux users can instead install a `.deb` package from the latest GitHub release (https://github.com/AprilNEA/OpenLogi/releases/latest) using `sudo dpkg -i openlogi-*.deb`.
summary.pros: OpenLogi keeps a light native Rust/GPUI footprint, treats Linux as a first-class platform, and stores all settings in one syncable TOML file. It supports assigning gesture roles to any physical button, per-application profile overlays, and a scriptable CLI alongside the GUI. Device-specific controls include DPI presets, SmartShift wheel settings, keyboard RGB lighting, and detailed UVC webcam image adjustments.
summary.cons: The project is explicitly marked as under active development and not yet stable, meaning features and configuration format may change before a stable release. Pre-built Linux packages require GLIBC 2.35 or newer (an Ubuntu 22.04 baseline), which could limit compatibility with older Linux distributions.
summary.fit: OpenLogi may suit users who want a native, open-source, cross-platform replacement for Logitech Options+ with scriptable configuration, particularly on Linux where Options+ has no official client. It is not affiliated with Logitech, so it could be less suitable for users who need official vendor support or a fully stabilized release.

repos.name: volcengine / OpenViking
repos.description: Self-evolving Context Database for AI Agents. Unify Agent Memory, Knowledge RAG and Skills.

summary.goal: OpenViking is an open-source context database for AI agents that stores memories, resources, and skills as a virtual filesystem addressed via the `viking://` protocol, letting agents browse context with commands such as `ls`, `tree`, and `find` instead of querying a vector store. Content is organized into three loading tiers — L0 abstract, L1 overview, L2 details — loaded on demand, and the main project is licensed under AGPLv3.
summary.usage: Install with `pip install openviking --upgrade`, which requires Python 3.10 or higher, then run `openviking-server init` to launch an interactive wizard that configures providers, models, and the `ov.conf` file. The install also includes an `ov` client CLI for interacting with a running server.
summary.pros: OpenViking version 0.3.22 has been evaluated on LoCoMo and tau2-bench benchmarks. Reported results show 80-83% LoCoMo accuracy across three agent integrations, up from 24-57% under native memory, with input token reductions of 34.3-91.0% and query latency reductions of 58.45-66.10%; tau2-bench task success increased by +6.87 percentage points for retail and +11.87 for airline scenarios.
summary.cons: The desktop OpenViking Helper companion app is documented as still in beta, currently limited to macOS and Windows x64 platforms, which suggests broader operating-system support may not yet be available.
summary.fit: The project appears suited to teams integrating agent memory and context retrieval into tools such as Claude Code, Codex, OpenClaw, Hermes, Cursor, and MCP clients, though the README notes the project is still in its early stages, implying interfaces and capabilities may continue to evolve.

repos.name: semantica-agi / semantica
repos.description: Graph-Native Infrastructure for Context and Accountable AI Systems

summary.goal: Semantica is a graph-native infrastructure library that ingests enterprise data, builds a Context Graph and knowledge graph (KG), and runs deterministic reasoning, ontology management, and decision provenance over it.
summary.usage: Install Semantica with `pip install semantica`, then use Python (e.g., `from semantica.context import ContextGraph`) to ingest data, record decisions, and query the graph; run `semantica doctor` to verify the install.
summary.pros: Semantica includes deterministic reasoning engines (forward chaining, Rete, Datalog, SPARQL) that work without an LLM, W3C PROV-O provenance on every fact, polyglot RDF/LPG graph storage, and built-in conflict detection and deduplication.
summary.cons: Semantica's Rete engine currently uses an alpha-node condition matcher described as intentionally simple, so its output should be validated against your own rule set before use in a production compliance gate.
summary.fit: Semantica targets regulated, high-stakes domains such as finance, healthcare, legal, and government, requiring Python 3.8+ and self-hosted deployment (https://github.com/semantica-agi/semantica), positioned as an alternative to enterprise SaaS knowledge platforms.

repos.name: xai-org / x-algorithm
repos.description: Algorithm powering the For You feed on X

summary.goal: This repository (xai-org/x-algorithm) contains the core code that determines which posts appear in the For You feed on X. It combines in-network posts from followed accounts, retrieved via Thunder, with out-of-network posts discovered through Phoenix retrieval and SimClusters, then filters and ranks the combined candidates using a transformer-based model called Phoenix.
summary.usage: The code is meant for inspection and experimentation rather than standalone deployment. Configuration defaults, including scoring weights, are set in home-mixer/params/param.rs. The phoenix/ directory ships a Cargo workspace and a pyproject.toml with a QUICKSTART.md guide and synthetic data generation, letting a small version of Phoenix be trained and served end-to-end.
summary.pros: Ranking and visibility filtering are documented as separate systems with distinct inputs, and the final score is computed transparently as Final Score = Σ (weight_i × P(action_i)) over predicted action probabilities. A companion Under the Hood tool at https://x.com/i/under_the_hood lets users view the labels applied to their own account and posts.
summary.cons: A limited set of files, such as Grox LLM prompts and some botmaker rules, are withheld from the repository to reduce the risk of gaming the system, so the published code may not fully reflect every production rule. Separately, pre-scoring filters drop posts older than 48 hours, so the pipeline is not built to surface older content.
summary.fit: Given its focus on transparency into ranking and filtering logic rather than turnkey deployment, the project appears best suited to people auditing, studying, or critiquing how X's For You feed selects and orders posts, rather than teams seeking a general-purpose, deployable recommendation system. It is licensed under the Apache License 2.0.

repos.name: vorssaint / vorssaint-utils
repos.description: Free and open-source macOS menu bar toolkit.

summary.goal: Vorssaint is a free, open-source macOS menu bar application that consolidates utilities such as a per-app volume mixer, system monitor, window snapping, app switcher, Dock previews, clipboard history, text snippets, a file shelf, and an uninstaller into one icon, aiming to replace several separate paid Mac utility apps.
summary.usage: Vorssaint can be installed via Homebrew with `brew install --cask vorssaint`, or by downloading the disk image from https://github.com/vorssaint/vorssaint-utils/releases and dragging it into Applications. Developers can build it from source by cloning the repository and running `./build.sh` (or `./build.sh --install` to also install and launch it); Xcode Command Line Tools are required for building.
summary.pros: Individual features can be installed or uninstalled separately, so unused features stop loading and consume no CPU, memory or energy. Permissions are requested only for the features that need them and are explained in plain language. Releases are signed with an Apple Developer ID and notarized, and the project is released under the GPL-3.0-or-later license.
summary.cons: Vorssaint requires a Mac with Apple Silicon and macOS 14 Sonoma or newer, so it does not run on older macOS versions or Intel-based Macs. Some functionality also depends on granting macOS permissions such as Accessibility or Screen Recording, and Full Disk Access is needed for deeper cleaner and uninstaller scans.
summary.fit: Given its described local-first design with no account, analytics or tracking, the tool appears best suited to privacy-conscious Mac users on recent Apple Silicon hardware who want to replace multiple paid single-purpose utilities with one free, open-source menu bar app. Because of its stated macOS 14+ and Apple Silicon requirements, it likely is not usable on older or Intel-based Macs.

repos.name: modular / modular
repos.description: The Modular Platform (includes MAX & Mojo)

summary.goal: This repository hosts open-source components of the Modular Platform, described as a unified platform for AI development and deployment. It includes the MAX Framework and the Mojo Language, covering the compiler, standard library, accelerator library, inference server, and model pipelines documented in the repo.
summary.usage: Getting started with the MAX framework involves the quickstart guide at https://max.modular.com/get-started, used for serving a model. Getting started with Mojo involves the quickstart guide at https://mojolang.org/docs/manual/quickstart/. Contributions to the Mojo standard library, MAX accelerator library, or MAX model architectures should begin by reading CONTRIBUTING.md.
summary.pros: The repo lists distinct components: the Mojo compiler, Mojo standard library, MAX accelerator library, an MAX inference server with an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, Python-based MAX model pipelines, and code examples. It accepts community contributions to the standard library, accelerator library, model architectures, and documentation.
summary.cons: Contributions to the Mojo compiler itself are not yet accepted, so external changes there may be limited. MAX usage and distribution follow a separate Modular Community License apart from the repository's Apache License v2.0 license, which could mean users need to review third-party library licenses themselves.
summary.fit: Given its coverage of an inference server, model pipelines, and a systems language compiler, the project appears aimed at teams building and deploying AI applications who are comfortable managing multiple licenses and validating third-party dependencies themselves.

repos.name: cactus-compute / needle
repos.description: 14MB foundation model for tiny devices; phones, wearables, smart home, and robots.

summary.goal: Needle 2 is an open 45M-parameter model for tool calling, device use, and structured extraction, distributed as a single 14MB binary that runs a full session in about 28MB of RAM. This repository is the Python package for inference, LoRA fine-tuning, and export; on cited benchmarks it trades wins with small models such as FunctionGemma 270M, LFM2.5 230M, and Apple FM while being 5x to 70x smaller.
summary.usage: After installing with `pip install cactus-needle`, developers decorate a Python function as a tool and call a run method so the model selects and executes it, returning output as structured data; a separate extraction call with a Pydantic model returns a typed object from text. The `needle playground` command opens a browser UI, by default at `http://127.0.0.1:7860`, for testing tools interactively.
summary.pros: Weights are baked into the single 14MB engine, so inference needs no separate model files and no network access. Every response carries a calibrated confidence score, and built-in tool retrieval narrows a large declared catalogue to the top five most relevant tools per turn. A 256-token sliding window with pinned tool keys keeps total runtime memory near 28MB regardless of conversation length.
summary.cons: The base runtime install does not include the training stack, so fine-tuning or checkpoint export needs an additional installation step; the optional data-synthesis feature further depends on an external `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`, so a full fine-tuning workflow may require more setup than the base install alone.
summary.fit: Given the small binary size, low memory footprint, and documented offline setup for air-gapped devices, the package appears suited to developers building tool-calling agents for resource-constrained or on-device deployments; ready-made environments such as smart_home and media_player suggest a fit for adapting tool surfaces to a product.

repos.name: debpalash / VoiceStudio
repos.description: VoiceStudio is the open-source, fully-local ElevenLabs alternative — voice cloning, voice design, video dubbing, dictation, transcription & audiobook creation in 646 languages.

summary.goal: VoiceStudio is a locally run application for cloning voices, dubbing video, dictating text, and producing long-form audio such as stories and audiobooks, running on the user's own hardware (macOS, Windows, Linux, and Docker) without requiring an account, API key, subscription, or usage meter for the local workflow.
summary.usage: Users download a packaged release for their platform (macOS 13.3+ Apple Silicon, Windows 10/11 x64, Linux x86_64, or Docker) and follow the platform guide, or run it via Docker with `docker run -d -p 127.0.0.1:3900:3900 -v omnivoice-data:/app/omnivoice_data --name voicestudio palashdeb/omnivoice-studio:stable`. To run from source, developers install Node 20+/Bun and Python 3.11+, then `git clone https://github.com/debpalash/VoiceStudio.git`, run `bun install`, and `bun run desktop`; the desktop launcher configures Python dependencies automatically on first run.
summary.pros: VoiceStudio offers 16 TTS engines, 11 ASR engines, and a 646-language catalogue, with multiple interfaces including a desktop app, a local REST/SSE/WebSocket API, an OpenAI-compatible audio API, and an MCP server. Storage stays local by default, and the local workflow needs no account, API key, subscription, or usage meter.
summary.cons: The default OmniVoice engine's pretrained weights are CC-BY-NC licensed with a separately licensed audio tokenizer, so commercial use of generated audio requires reviewing model-specific terms beyond VoiceStudio's AGPL-3.0 application license.
summary.fit: VoiceStudio targets private, offline, self-hosted, or high-volume voice work, contrasted with hosted voice services suited to fast setup without local model management; since users must supply hardware and manage updates and disk themselves, it likely suits those who prioritize local control over managed convenience.

repos.name: marin-community / marin
repos.description: Open-source framework for the research and development of foundation models.

summary.goal: Marin is presented as a research program, software platform, and community for developing foundation models, focused on training large language models across data curation, tokenization, pretraining, posttraining, and evaluation. Current work targets pretraining and posttraining a mixture-of-experts model at 5e24 model-FLOPs with 500 billion+ total parameters, intended for tasks important to scientists and researchers.
summary.usage: Getting started involves installing Marin, training a tiny language model, and optionally running a larger DCLM 1B/1x experiment. Documentation is hosted at https://marin.readthedocs.io/en/latest/, and community discussion happens on the Marin Discord at https://discord.gg/J9CTk7pqcM. The README's example script defines dependent steps and runs them with `StepRunner().run([lower(nano_tinystories_model)])`.
summary.pros: Marin documents its process openly, recording experiments and decisions — including failed experiments — under an open-development approach. For its Delphi scaling suite, spanning 3e18 to 1e23 FLOPs, Marin has openly released checkpoints, training-mixture pipelines, and recipe code on Hugging Face and GitHub. Marin was also previously used to train an 8B parameter model that outperformed Llama 3.1 8B on Marin's own benchmark suite, plus a separate 32B model.
summary.cons: The README's example script imports several external packages alongside Marin's own modules, including fray.cluster and levanter.optim, suggesting that adopting Marin requires installing and coordinating multiple interdependent libraries rather than a single self-contained package.
summary.fit: Marin appears best suited to research teams pursuing large-scale foundation-model pretraining with access to substantial compute, since current work targets multi-hundred-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts models. Core contributors are affiliated with Stanford CRFM and Open Athena, suggesting an academic, open-research orientation rather than a turnkey commercial product.

repos.name: apache / maka
repos.description: Apache Maka (Incubating) is a high-performance agent workspace that keeps a complete record of everything it did.

summary.goal: Apache Maka (Incubating) is presented as a high-performance agent workspace that keeps a complete, append-only record of everything it does, via a RuntimeEvent log capturing model messages, tool calls, and permission decisions. The README states results are benchmarked against other harnesses on the same model with an official verifier, with per-task results published in `docs/eval/`.
summary.usage: To build from source: `git clone https://github.com/apache/maka.git`, then `npm ci` and `npm run dev` to start the Desktop dev environment with HMR. Stated requirements are Node.js 22.19+ (CI uses Node.js 24), npm 11, Git, and ripgrep; Direct Peer/Peer Mesh development additionally needs Rust stable 1.98+.
summary.pros: According to the README, the RuntimeEvent log is the authoritative runtime record rather than just the UI or next prompt, sessions/settings/run records stay local while users supply their own model (cloud API, local model, or gateway), and Desktop, TUI/CLI, and Eval share a single Runtime Host execution authority.
summary.cons: The README notes Apache Maka has not made an official Apache release yet, so no signed source archive currently exists as the release artifact. It also states the project is under ASF incubation and active development, so data formats, CLI commands, and experimental capabilities may still change.
summary.fit: Based on the stated Desktop Nightly platform support (signed macOS Apple Silicon/Intel builds; unsigned Windows x64 and Linux x64/arm64 previews) and the explicit note that Nightly builds are not intended for production use, this suggests best fit for developers and testers building or evaluating agent harnesses locally.

summary.goal: According to the README, vphone-cli is a command-line tool that boots a virtual iPhone using Apple's Virtualization.framework, built on PCC research VM infrastructure.
summary.usage: It can be installed with `brew install zqxwce/tap/vphone-cli`, or built from source by cloning `https://github.com/Lakr233/vphone-cli.git` with `--recurse-submodules` and running the setup and build scripts. Running `vphone-cli vm create myphone -V jb` followed by `vphone-cli vm launch myphone` is described as provisioning and booting a virtual iPhone end-to-end.
summary.pros: According to the README, a single command appears to automate the full pipeline—download, patch, DFU restore, CFW install, and first boot—which could make setup comparatively fast. Five firmware patch variants (`less`, `regular`, `dev`, `jb`, `exp`) offer graduated levels of security bypass, and a host control socket seems intended to support programmatic automation for AI-driven end-to-end testing.
summary.cons: Running vphone-cli requires relaxing SIP/AMFI protections on the host, which likely represents a meaningful security trade-off since it lowers macOS's built-in protections. The README also documents what appears to be a known upstream bug in ldid-procursus up to version 2.1.5-procursus7 that can hang the `cfw install` step, suggesting that a from-source rebuild (`brew install --HEAD ldid-procursus`) may currently be needed as a workaround.
summary.fit: Given the stated Apple Silicon and macOS 15+ host prerequisites, along with the required SIP/AMFI relaxation, this tool seems best suited to security researchers or developers already comfortable lowering system protections for research purposes. The README notes that nested virtualization is unsupported, implying it likely cannot run inside another virtual machine.

repos.name: public-apis / public-apis
repos.description: A collective list of free APIs

summary.goal: The public-apis/public-apis repository is a community-curated, categorized directory of free and public APIs for developers, spanning domains such as Animals, Business, Games & Comics, and Weather, intended to help developers discover public APIs for their own projects.
summary.usage: Developers browse the Index to jump to a category section, then follow each listed API's own link for that provider's documentation and signup; contributions follow the Contributing Guide and are submitted via Pull Request, with existing entries tracked through GitHub Issues (https://github.com/public-apis/public-apis/issues) and Pull Requests (https://github.com/public-apis/public-apis/pulls).
summary.pros: It covers 51 distinct categories with hundreds of entries, and each entry lists whether an API requires an apiKey or OAuth, supports HTTPS, and supports CORS, letting developers quickly gauge integration requirements before visiting a provider's site.
summary.cons: The README does not verify the reliability or terms of individual third-party APIs, and since numerous entries list CORS or Auth as 'Unknown,' documentation completeness across entries may be inconsistent, so users likely need to check each provider's own site before relying on it for production use.
summary.fit: This resource appears best suited to developers browsing or prototyping with free public APIs across many domains, rather than teams needing a single vetted, installable dependency, since integration reliability still depends on each individual third-party provider.

repos.name: megadose / holehe
repos.description: holehe allows you to check if the mail is used on different sites like twitter, instagram and will retrieve information on sites with the forgotten password function.
